description: Programmable cryptography at MSN-chat pace: garbled circuits, SNARKs, FHE and ORAM as one toolkit, after the 0xPARC primer, with a live SHA-256 demo.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. Hash a secret in the demo above.
disclosure: How to read this: a first-pass walkthrough of "Programmable Cryptography: Four Easy Pieces" by Evan Chen, Brian Lawrence, and Yan X Zhang (0xPARC, 2025), summarized under fair use with credit. The learner lines and pacing are AI; the SHA-256 demo hashes for real.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader recognizes the vocabulary of programmable cryptography but can't yet predict what the mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain programmable cryptography in plain language and predict its behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model and stop short of a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you close the window: pop quiz, 7 questions, no grades. The demo up there keeps hashing if you need it.

questions.q: A team wants to prove a private dataset's average is above 50 without showing the data. How does a second-generation cryptographer start?

options.t: write the average check as code and hand it to a general primitive
options.why: That's the gen 2 move: the primitive takes any function you can write as code, so you compile the problem you have. The bill for that generality comes later in the chat, and it's steep.

options.t: design a fresh protocol just for averages, the way Yao did for incomes
options.why: That's the first-generation habit the chat starts from: RSA for signing, a bespoke protocol for the millionaires. Programmable means you stop inventing an algorithm per problem.

options.t: wait for a primitive that ships with averaging built in as a feature
options.why: That's the alarm clock, one device per job. The smartphone half of the analogy is a single general primitive that runs whatever function you compile for it.

options.t: put the dataset on a blockchain so a smart contract can check it
options.why: Blockchains show up at the end of the chat as the demand that pulled the practical work forward. Nothing in the definition needs a chain, only primitives you program for any function.

questions.q: In the demo, add one space to the end of "attack at dawn". What happens on the sha256(M) line?

options.t: a completely different 64-hex-digit digest replaces the old one
options.why: The demo hashes the box's exact bytes, space included, and any change, even one byte, gives SHA-256 an unrelated digest of the same 64 digits. Delete the space and the old digest comes back: same bytes, same hash.

options.t: nothing changes, since a trailing space isn't part of the secret
options.why: The demo hashes the input exactly as typed, with no trimming, so the space is one more byte of M. Type it and watch the whole line rewrite.

options.t: the old digest stays, with only its last couple of digits changed
options.why: If a small edit made a small change, the digest would leak which bytes of M you touched. The hash tip on the page says any one-byte change gives a different hash, and the demo rewrites every digit.

options.t: the digest grows by two hex digits, one byte for the new space
options.why: SHA-256 always prints 256 bits, 64 hex digits, whatever goes in: an empty box and a paragraph get the same length. The digest's size belongs to the hash, and M's size never shows.

questions.q: Two shops run 2PC on their customer lists to learn whether they share any customers. What does each shop walk away knowing?

options.t: the yes-or-no answer and its own list, and nothing else of the other's
options.why: Each party keeps its input and both get only F(x1, x2), the same deal the millionaires got. Push on it, though: the answer itself says something. If it's no, each shop now knows none of its customers are on the other list.

options.t: nothing at all, since every gate of the circuit runs on encrypted values
options.why: Half right. The gates run blind, but the output gets decoded at the end: the millionaires walked away knowing the winner. A protocol that told nobody anything would compute F for no one.

options.t: whatever a trusted referee who saw both lists decides to announce
options.why: That referee is the setup 2PC deletes. Nobody ever holds both inputs: one shop garbles the circuit and the other evaluates it blind.

options.t: both lists, encrypted so that only the two shops can read them
options.why: If either shop could read the other's list, the protocol would be pointless. Go back to the millionaires: both learn the winner and neither learns the other's number.

questions.q: The demo above hashes your secret M and prints sha256(M) live. What would a real SNARK add on top of what the demo already does?

options.t: it would prove i know some M behind that exact digest, without showing M
options.why: That's the statement shape from the chat: I know X such that F(X, Y) = Z, with F and the digest public and only the witness hidden. The demo gives you the public half; the SNARK adds the proof of knowledge.

options.t: it would encrypt the digest too, so nobody but you can read the hash
options.why: The digest stays public on purpose: it's the reference a verifier checks the proof against. Secrecy covers only the witness M, the thing you typed into the box.

options.t: it would let the verifier run sha256 backwards and recover M to check it
options.why: Nobody recovers M; that would defeat the exercise. The verifier ends up convinced you know a preimage while learning nothing about it, which is the whole trick the demo is teeing up.

options.t: it would swap sha256 for a faster hash so the proof is cheap to make
options.why: F stays whatever the statement needs, here SHA-256 encoded as equations. And proving stays expensive: the chat's number is millions of times the cost of just running the computation.

questions.q: A friend says: once my records sit FHE-encrypted on the server, the server learns nothing about me. What's the hole in that?

options.t: the server still watches which encrypted records get asked for, and when
options.why: Encryption hides the bytes, and the access pattern leaks anyway: open the same record every morning and the server knows something about you. ORAM is the fix, scrambling each request into a batch of reads and writes, and it pays for that in extra traffic.

options.t: the server gets to decrypt the ciphertext once it computes on it
options.why: Then FHE would be useless. The chat's loop is encrypt, let the server compute on the ciphertext, decrypt the result yourself, and the server reads nothing at any step.

options.t: there's no hole: encrypted data and encrypted compute hide everything
options.why: The chat names the leak right after FHE: even with the data encrypted, the server watches your access pattern. That leftover is the whole reason ORAM is the fourth piece.

options.t: the server can see the key, because FHE has to send it along
options.why: The key stays with you: you encrypt, the server computes on Enc(x), and you decrypt what comes back. The leak your friend missed sits in which ciphertexts you ask for.

questions.q: If this toolkit can compute on secrets and prove any statement you can encode, why did it spend a decade as mostly theory?

options.t: the overhead: proving costs up to millions of times the computation itself
options.why: The primer is blunt about that number. It stayed mostly theory until blockchains and other decentralized systems demanded it hard enough to pull the practical work forward.

options.t: it needed special trusted chips that most servers didn't ship with yet
options.why: Backwards: this toolkit exists so you never have to trust a chip. Every guarantee here comes from protocols and math; betting on trusted hardware is the TEE, the far end of the spectrum.

options.t: the security proofs weren't finished, so nobody dared to deploy it in production
options.why: The theory was the mature half; constructions existed for years. Implementation is what lagged, because the costs were brutal until real demand showed up.

options.t: encoding real programs as equations stayed an unsolved research problem
options.why: Turning F into equations is standard machinery, it's how the SNARK statement gets built at all. The bottleneck was the sheer cost of proving, and demand is what finally moved it.

questions.q: Last one. The millionaires skip 2PC and send both incomes into a TEE that announces the winner. What did they give up?

options.t: secrecy from math alone: one chip now holds both incomes, and they trust it
options.why: 2PC's promise is that nobody ever holds both inputs. The TEE puts both in one place and asks you to trust the chip and whoever built it: the same goal, with the trust moved from protocols and math onto hardware.

options.t: nothing, since the enclave keeps both incomes hidden from everyone too
options.why: Partly right: the enclave is meant to hide them. But that's the bet. 2PC needs nobody to hold both numbers, and the TEE needs the chip to keep its promise, which is exactly the trust the chat's last bubble says this toolkit avoids.

options.t: the answer, because a TEE can hold the data but can't compare two numbers
options.why: The chat offers the TEE as another way to compute on data nobody should see, so the comparison runs fine. What changes is where the trust lives, the axis the chat's last bubble draws.

options.t: speed, because the TEE has to garble the comparison circuit gate by gate
options.why: Garbling gate by gate is 2PC's engine, the very machinery the TEE skips. The TEE trades that machinery for trust in a chip.

messages.html: people keep saying "programmable cryptography" like it's one thing. RSA is cryptography, MPC is cryptography. what's the second word doing?

0xPARC coined it for the second generation of crypto, roughly the last 15 years. First-generation crypto hand-builds a protocol per problem: RSA signs a message, and Yao's millionaire problem gets its own bespoke protocol to compare two incomes. Second-generation crypto hands you primitives you can program for any function you can write as code.

Their analogy: it's the jump from single-purpose hardware (a digital alarm clock) to a general-purpose one (a smartphone that runs whatever you compile for it). You stop inventing a new algorithm per problem and start compiling the problem you have.

The primer picks four: 2PC (two-party computation), SNARKs (succinct proofs), FHE (compute on encrypted data), and ORAM (hide which data you touch). Two of those already have rooms here, so I'll wire them up as we go.

Two people compute F(x1, x2) where each knows only their own input, and neither learns the other's. Yao's millionaire problem is the classic: F is "who earns more," the inputs are the two incomes, and both walk away knowing the winner but not the number. The engine underneath is a garbled circuit (one party encrypts a boolean circuit gate by gate, the other evaluates it blind) plus oblivious transfer. Scale 2PC past two parties and you land on the MPC one room over.
you keep saying proofs. what's a SNARK?

Read a signature as a proof: Alice's signature proves "I know Alice's private key." A SNARK generalizes that to a proof of any statement shaped like "I know X such that F(X, Y) = Z," with F, Y, Z public, once you encode F as equations. The primer's headline example is "I know M such that sha(M) = Y." PLONK is one such scheme. Try the hash half live:

A SNARK proves "I know X such that F(X) = Y" while revealing nothing about X. Here F is SHA-256. Type a secret M and the page hashes it live (real Web Crypto). A SNARK would let you prove you know some M with this exact digest, without ever showing M.

messages.html: so the hash is public but the M behind it stays secret. and FHE + ORAM?

FHE you've met: encrypt your data, let a server compute on the ciphertext, decrypt the result, and the server reads nothing. The primer's example is private machine translation: send Enc(x), get back Enc(translation). ORAM is the piece with no room here yet. Even with the data encrypted, the server still watches your access pattern: which records you read, how often, which ones together. Oblivious RAM scrambles each request into a batch of reads and writes, so the server can't tell which one you actually wanted.
if it does all that, why isn't it everywhere?

Cost, and the primer is blunt about it: proving a computation in a SNARK can run millions of times the cost of just doing the computation. For a decade it was mostly theory with little implementation, until blockchains and other decentralized systems started demanding it and pulled the practical work forward.
so the throughline is: one toolkit, privacy and proofs from math instead of trusted hardware.

That's the frame. 2PC and MPC, SNARKs, FHE, and ORAM are different tools, but each earns its guarantee from protocols and math, the far end from a TEE and the chip it asks you to trust. Same goal, compute on data nobody should see, with a different bet on where the trust lives.

got it. the four pieces are one compiler target. thanks.
